title: Task 1
text:
Task 1 examined whether adding uncertainty information made the underlying spatial pattern in an EEG topoplot more difficult to recognize. On each trial, participants saw a target ERP pattern and two alternative topoplots. They selected the alternative that most closely matched the target. One alternative represented the same ERP-pattern class as the target, while the other represented a different class.
The task included three characteristic ERP patterns: MMN, P3, and N170. Each was shown using each of the seven visualization types. This produced 21 trials per participant, each on separate page. Trial order was randomized separately for every participant.






Figure 1: Example comparison trial. Participants selected the alternative whose spatial pattern most closely matched the target.

Trial reconstruction and presentation order

Trial information was reconstructed from the survey records and joined with each participant’s responses using participant, trial, and question identifiers.



Code

  dplyr::select(ID, A125_02) %>%
  tidyr::separate_rows(A125_02, sep = "\n") %>%
  dplyr::filter(A125_02 != "") %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    ID,
    position = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "position")),
    trial    = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "trial")),
    question = get_field(A125_02, "question"),
    stimulus = get_field(A125_02, "stimulus"),
    expected = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "expected")),
    answered = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "answered")),
    correct  = as.integer(get_field(A125_02, "correct"))
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(ID, position)

task1_design <- data %>%
  dplyr::select(ID, A124_01) %>%
  tidyr::separate_rows(A124_01, sep = "\n") %>%
  dplyr::filter(A124_01 != "") %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    ID,
    trial       = as.integer(get_field(A124_01, "trial")),
    question    = get_field(A124_01, "question"),
    vistype     = get_field(A124_01, "vistype"),

title: Task 1
text:
Accuracy analysis

Every response was coded as correct (1) or incorrect (0).
The analysis contains 2,394 responses: 114 participants × 21 trials.
Visualization type was treated as a categorical variable, with the basic topoplot as the reference condition.
Presentation position was represented by the centered variable position_c, calculated as position - mean(position). Because positions ranged from 1 to 21, their mean was 11. Thus, position_c = 0 represents position 11, negative values represent earlier trials, and positive values represent later trials. This variable tests whether accuracy changed linearly as participants progressed through the task.
No responses were excluded for missing values. All 2,394 reconstructed records contained accuracy, visualization type, ERP pattern, presentation position, target stimulus, and distractor stimulus.
Stimulus assignment was incomplete but overlapping across participants. Across their 21 trials, participants saw 12–20 unique target stimuli (median 16), 13–20 unique distractors (median 15), and 18–28 unique stimulus identities across both roles (median 23). No participant saw all 30 stimulus identities. Because specific targets and distractors may differ in difficulty, this design motivates separate target- and distractor-stimulus random intercepts in the inferential model.



Code
task1_model <- task1 %>%
  transmute(
    ID = factor(ID),
    trial = factor(trial),
    vistype = relevel(factor(vistype), ref = "basic"),
    pattern = relevel(factor(pattern), ref = "MMN"),
    stimulus = factor(stimulus),
    wrong_image = factor(wrong_image),
    position = as.integer(position),
    correct = as.integer(correct)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(correct),
    !is.na(position),
    !is.na(vistype),
    !is.na(pattern),
    !is.na(stimulus),
    !is.na(wrong_image)
  ) %>%
  mutate(position_c = position - mean(position))



Observed accuracy

Accuracy was calculated as correct responses divided by all responses (correct / (correct + incorrect)). Each visualization type had 342 responses (114 participants × 3 trials). This is an unadjusted pooled proportion.
For the descriptive uncertainty display, each participant contributed one mean accuracy per visualization type, calculated from their three trials. Because every participant contributed the same number of trials, the across-participant mean equals the pooled proportion above.
The dark-blue region shows the two-sided 95% t-confidence interval around the across-participant mean; opacity decreases beyond that interval.



Code
task1_gradient_participants <- task1_model |>
  group_by(ID, vistype) |>
  summarise(
    participant_accuracy = mean(correct),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

task1_gradient_order <- task1_gradient_participants |>
  group_by(vistype) |>
  summarise(mean_accuracy = mean(participant_accuracy), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(mean_accuracy) |>
  pull(vistype) |>
  as.character()

task1_gradient_summary <- task1_gradient_participants |>
  group_by(vistype) |>
  summarise(
    n_participants = n(),
    mean_accuracy = mean(participant_accuracy),
    se_accuracy = sd(participant_accuracy) / sqrt(n_participants),
    df = n_participants - 1,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    vistype = factor(vistype, levels = task1_gradient_order),
    y_position = as.numeric(vistype),
    lower_95 = mean_accuracy - qt(0.975, df) * se_accuracy,
    upper_95 = mean_accuracy + qt(0.975, df) * se_accuracy
  ) |>
  arrange(vistype)

task1_response_counts <- task1_model |>
  group_by(vistype) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_correct = sum(correct == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_incorrect = sum(correct == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    pooled_accuracy = mean(correct, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

  left_join(
    task1_gradient_summary |>

Observed comparison-task accuracy summarized from participant-level means. Each participant contributes one mean from three trials per visualization type. The black line and label show the across-participant mean; the dark-blue region shows its two-sided 95% t-confidence interval. This unadjusted description does not replace the mixed model below, which accounts for ERP pattern, presentation position, participant, target stimulus, and distractor stimulus.






Population-average accuracy

A logistic mixed-effects model estimated the probability of a correct response:
correct ~ vistype + pattern + position_c +
  (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | wrong_image)
Some participants were generally more accurate than others. Because every participant completed 21 trials, we added a participant random intercept, which allows each participant to have their own baseline accuracy. The model then examines whether accuracy changed with visualization type or trial position across participants.
ERP pattern was included as a fixed effect, so visualization comparisons account for systematic accuracy differences among MMN, N170, and P3 trials.
Target and distractor stimuli were included as separate random intercepts. This gives each image its own baseline difficulty in each role and prevents unusually easy or difficult images from being mistaken for visualization effects.
These probabilities estimate average accuracy for each visualization type across the modeled participant and stimulus populations. They were calculated at the average trial position, averaged equally across the three ERP patterns, and integrated over modeled differences among participants, target stimuli, and distractor stimuli.







NoteChoosing how to summarize predicted accuracy





There are three ways to summarize the model:








Option
Calculation
What it describes




1
Set participant and stimulus differences to zero.
Average-baseline participants and stimuli.


2
Average over the fitted participants, targets, and distractors.
The levels observed in this study.


3
Average across modeled participant and stimulus differences.
The modeled participant and stimulus populations.



We chose option 3 because our research question concerns average performance across participant and stimulus populations, not only average-baseline or observed levels (Hu et al., 1998; Hedeker et al., 2018).
Estimand sensitivity check. Across visualization types, the largest difference between the selected population-average probability and the zero-random-effect probability was 7.1 percentage points; the largest difference from the fitted participant-and-stimulus average was 0.4 percentage points. The reporting choice therefore does not materially change the pattern of results.
This does not make the sample representative of all EEG researchers.









NoteWhy participant-specific random slopes were not retained





We tested whether the effect of trial position differed between participants by adding a participant-specific position slope: (1 + position_c | ID), while retaining the ERP pattern and stimulus terms. The model produced a singular fit and could not estimate this additional variation:

The estimated variance of the position slopes was 0.00018.
The estimated correlation between the baseline accuracy and position slopes was -1.00.

Together, these boundary estimates indicate that the data did not contain enough information to estimate participant baseline differences and participant-specific position effects separately.
We also considered participant-specific effects for visualization type. However, each participant provided only three responses for each visualization. Modeling the seven-level visualization factor would require six additional slopes and their covariances, which the available responses could not support reliably.
We therefore retained the simpler random-intercept model. This does not show that the position and visualization effects are identical for every participant. It means only that these data cannot reliably estimate how those effects differ between participants.

Model details:


Model: Binomial mixed-effects model with a logit link: correct ~ vistype + pattern + position_c + (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | wrong_image).


Reference visualization: Basic topoplot.


ERP pattern: Predictions were averaged equally across MMN, N170, and P3.


Trial position: Predicted accuracy was calculated at the average presentation position.


Random effects: Predictions were averaged across the modeled distributions of participant baseline accuracy and target- and distractor-stimulus difficulty.


Confidence intervals: A separate 95% confidence interval was calculated for each visualization type from 10,000 simulated sets of fixed-effect estimates generated with MASS::mvrnorm().


Limitation: The estimated participant and stimulus random-intercept variances were treated as fixed when calculating these intervals.

These comparisons estimate the population-average accuracy difference between each visualization and the basic topoplot. Confidence intervals crossing zero indicate that the corresponding visualization is not clearly different from Basic at the 95% confidence level.

make_likert_estimate_plot <- function(
  question_name,
  show_x = TRUE,
  show_labels = TRUE
) {

  plot_data <- likert_estimates |>
    filter(question == question_name) |>
    mutate(
      colour_group = if_else(vistype == "basic", "basic", "other"),
    
      display_label = unname(
        likert_display_labels[as.character(vistype)]
      ),
    
      vistype = factor(
        vistype,
        levels = rev(likert_vistype_order)
      )
    )

  p <- ggplot(
    plot_data,
      aes(
    x = estimated_rating,
    y = vistype,
    colour = colour_group
  )
  ) +
    geom_errorbar(
      aes(
        xmin = lower_ci,
        xmax = upper_ci
      ),
      orientation = "y",
      width = 0.12,
      linewidth = 0.55
    ) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +

    # Estimated values
    geom_text(
      aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", estimated_rating)),
      nudge_y = 0.32,
      vjust = 0.5,
      size = 30 / ggplot2::.pt
    ) +

    scale_colour_manual(
  values = c(
    basic = "#3B78B4",
    other = "#222222"
  ),
  guide = "none"
) +

    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = 1:5,
      labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))
    ) +

    # Hide ordinary y-axis labels
    scale_y_discrete(
      labels = NULL,
      expand = expansion(add = 0.5)
    ) +

      xlim = c(1, 5),
      clip = "off"
    ) +

    labs(
      title = unname(likert_panel_titles[question_name]),
      x = NULL,

title: Task 2
text:
Task 2 examined whether participants could combine information about estimated voltage and its uncertainty to locate a relevant spatial region. On each trial, participants saw one EEG topoplot and were asked to select the scalp region with the highest signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), defined as the absolute average-referenced voltage divided by its standard error. They responded using a separate scalp layout divided into 64 selectable regions.
The task included three characteristic ERP patterns: MMN, P3, and N170. Each was shown using each of the seven visualization types. This produced 21 trials per participant, each on a separate page. Trial order was randomized separately for every participant.






Figure 1: Example uncertainty-integration trial. Participants selected one of 64 regions after identifying the region with the highest SNR.

title: Task 2
text:
Response scoring and trial reconstruction

For each participan we reconstructed presentation order. Each participant went through 21 randomly shuffled pages.
For each trial, survey recorded the visualization, ERP stimulus shown and one region selected by participant. There were 64 regions on selectable grid.
The selected region was matched to the corresponding stimulus and its stored region score in regions.txt.
The region score represents |Voltage|/SE at that region. This calcaulation is actually more complicated.







NoteHow the 0–1 region score was calculated





For each stimulus, the scoring pipeline performed the following steps:

It loaded one average-referenced ERP case using the task, subject, time point, and condition recorded in task_configs_30_balanced. The fixed combinations were:



ERP pattern

MMN

It average-referenced the voltage across the \(N\) channels:
\[
V_i^{AR} = V_i - \frac{1}{N}\sum_j V_j.
\]
It calculated a polarity-independent, t-like signal-to-noise value at each channel:
\[
T_i = \frac{|V_i^{AR}|}{SE_i}.
\]
It interpolated the channel-level \(T_i\) values into a continuous topoplot grid. Only finite interpolated cells inside the visible head mask were retained.
It fitted the saved 64-region polygon template to the topoplot domain. For each region \(k\), it averaged all retained grid cells that were inside both the polygon and the head mask:
\[
R_k = \operatorname{mean}\{T(x,y):(x,y)\in\text{region}_k\}.
\]
It min–max normalized the 64 raw region scores separately within each stimulus:
\[
S_k = \frac{R_k - \min_j R_j}{\max_j R_j - \min_j R_j}.
\]
The weakest region therefore receives 0, the strongest receives 1, and other regions are positioned proportionally between them. Scores are rounded to two decimal places.

Implementation references. The stimulus-generation source is stored under UnfoldMakie/experiments/working/:

stimulus selection: stimuli_data.jl:213;
average referencing and channel score: region_detection/rereferencing.jl:96;
topoplot interpolation: region_detection/region_score_exports.jl:48;
polygon validation and fitting: get_regions.jl:19;
regional averaging: region_detection/scoring.jl:338;
normalization, rounding, and export: region_detection/region_score_exports.jl:7.

The polygon definitions are stored in experiments/figures/task2_topo_regions_64_eeg_aligned_pipeline28/regions.jl.

Descriptive detection scores

The analysis contains 2,394 responses: 114 participants x 21 trials. Each visualization type therefore has 342 responses: 114 participants x 3 ERP patterns.

text:
Detection-score analysis

The primary analysis uses the extended model:
score ~ vistype + pattern + position_c + (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus)
The outcome contains exact 0 and 1 values as well as intermediate scores. An ordered-beta model retains this graded information while supporting the complete closed interval from 0 to 1. A binary logistic model would instead treat every score below 1 as equally incorrect.
Every participant completed 21 trials, so responses from the same participant are related. Adding (1 | ID) gives each participant their own baseline detection performance while estimating common visualization, pattern, and presentation-position effects.
Some stimuli may be intrinsically easier to interpret than others. Adding (1 | stimulus) gives each stimulus its own baseline score, so visualization comparisons are not attributed to stimulus difficulty alone.
ERP pattern and centered presentation position adjust the visualization comparisons for the displayed pattern and for linear change as participants progressed through the task.
The simpler base model is shown first as a reference. It contains visualization type and a participant random intercept but does not adjust for pattern, presentation position, or differences among stimuli.

NoteWhy correlated participant-specific visualization slopes were not retained





We tested whether the effect of visualization type differed between participants by adding correlated participant-specific visualization effects: (1 + vistype | ID). The model could not estimate this full structure reliably:

It ended with convergence code 1, a non-positive-definite Hessian, and singular convergence.
The structure requires seven participant-level random coefficients and 28 variance–covariance parameters.
Each participant provided only three detection scores for each visualization type, which did not contain enough information to estimate all those parameters reliably.

We also tested simpler participant-specific structures:

A participant-specific position slope converged, but its estimated standard deviation was only 0.006.
A diagonal visualization structure, diag(0 + vistype | ID), converged with a positive-definite Hessian. It estimates separate participant-specific visualization variances without estimating their correlations.

We therefore retained participant and stimulus random intercepts in the primary model. This does not show that visualization effects are identical for every participant. It means that these data cannot reliably estimate the full correlated structure. The diagonal model remains available as a sensitivity analysis.

Model: Ordered-beta mixed model with a logit link: score ~ vistype + pattern + position_c + (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus).

text:
Completion-time analysis

Completion time was reconstructed from the 21 page-timing variables and linked to each trial by participant and presentation position.
Only non-missing positive times with an identified visualization type were retained. The descriptive table removes extreme times separately within each visualization type using the project’s IQR rule; the mixed model retains all positive times.
The model analyzes log completion time because trial times are positive and typically right-skewed:
log(time_sec) ~ vistype + position_c + (1 | ID)
The participant random intercept allows participants to have different typical response speeds. Presentation position adjusts for linear changes in speed across the 21 trials. Model estimates and confidence intervals are converted back from log time to seconds.

make_a305_intensity_figure <- function(
  plot_data,
  angle_x_labels = FALSE,
  fade_singletons = FALSE

  theme_panel_counts <- plot_data |>
    count(theme, name = "n_entries") |>
    arrange(desc(n_entries), theme)

  theme_panel_order <- theme_panel_counts$theme
  theme_panel_labels <- setNames(
    paste0(
      theme_panel_counts$theme,
      " (N = ",
      theme_panel_counts$n_entries,
      ")"
    ),
    theme_panel_counts$theme
  )

  plot_data <- plot_data |>
    group_by(theme, visualization) |>
    mutate(
      n_group = n(),
      point_alpha = if_else(fade_singletons & n_group == 1, 0.25, 0.8)
    ) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(theme = factor(theme, levels = theme_panel_order))

  boxplot_data <- if (fade_singletons) {
    filter(plot_data, n_group > 1)
  } else {
    plot_data
  }

  x_axis_text <- if (angle_x_labels) {
    ggtext::element_markdown(
      size = 20,
      angle = 30,
      hjust = 1,
      vjust = 1,
      lineheight = 0.9,
      margin = margin(t = 8)
    )
  } else {
    ggtext::element_markdown(
      size = 24,
      lineheight = 0.85,
      margin = margin(t = 6)
    )
  }

  ggplot(
    plot_data,
    aes(
      x = visualization,
      y = median_intensity,
      colour = visualization == "Basic",
      fill = visualization == "Basic"
    )
  ) +
    geom_boxplot(
      data = boxplot_data,
      width = 0.62,
      outlier.shape = NA,
      linewidth = 0.6

    ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(
      aes(alpha = point_alpha),
      size = 2.4,
      cex = 1.15,
      priority = "ascending",
      corral = "gutter",
      corral.width = 0.5
    ) +
    facet_wrap(
      vars(theme),
      scales = "free_x",
      ncol = 2,
      labeller = as_labeller(theme_panel_labels)
    ) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = visualization_axis_labels, drop = TRUE) +
    scale_colour_manual(
      values = c(`FALSE` = "#333333", `TRUE` = "#377EB8"),
      guide = "none"
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c(`FALSE` = "#D9D9D9", `TRUE` = "#B9D8F2"),
      guide = "none"
    ) +
    scale_alpha_identity() +
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = c(-2.15, 2.15),
      breaks = -2:2,
      labels = intensity_axis_labels,
      minor_breaks = NULL
    ) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = "Participant-level median evaluation intensity",
      caption = paste(
        "Points represent participants, not individual meaning units.",
        "Panel N is the number of plotted participant–visualization entries.",
        "−2 = strongly negative; +2 = strongly positive."
      )
    ) +
    theme_classic(base_family = "Lato", base_size = 18) +
    theme(
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 40),
      axis.text.x = x_axis_text,
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 16),
      axis.title.y = element_text(size = 40),
      axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
      panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.2, "lines"),

    )
}

Task 2
text:
Task 2 examined whether participants could combine information about estimated voltage and its uncertainty to locate a relevant spatial region. On each trial, participants saw one EEG topoplot and were asked to select the scalp region with the highest signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), defined as the absolute average-referenced voltage divided by its standard error. They responded using a separate scalp layout divided into 64 selectable regions.
The task included three characteristic ERP patterns: MMN, P3, and N170. Each was shown using each of the seven visualization types. This produced 21 trials per participant, each on a separate page. Trial order was randomized separately for every participant.

title: Task 1
text:
Bradley–Terry paired-choice sensitivity analysis
Task 1 is a paired-choice experiment: every trial presents one matching and one nonmatching candidate image. We therefore fitted a Bradley–Terry-style conditional logistic model as a sensitivity analysis. Unlike the primary accuracy model, this model assigns each of the 30 candidate images one shared attractiveness parameter regardless of whether that image is matching or nonmatching on a particular trial. It also adjusts for whether an image appeared as the second option.
The data were represented by two rows per trial, with one row for each candidate and one selected candidate within each participant–trial choice set. Visualization effects were estimated as interactions with matching-candidate status because visualization type is constant within a choice set and its main effect therefore cancels. Standard errors were clustered by participant to account for each participant’s 21 choices.

  transmute(
    ID = factor(ID),
    trial,
    choice_set = interaction(ID, trial, drop = TRUE),
    vistype = relevel(factor(vistype), ref = "basic"),
    pattern = relevel(factor(pattern), ref = "MMN"),
    position_c = position - mean(position),
    stimulus = as.character(stimulus),
    correct_image = as.character(correct_image),
    wrong_image = as.character(wrong_image),
    solution,
    answered,
    recorded_correct = correct,
    opt1,
    opt2
  )

task1_bt_expected_opt1 <- if_else(
  task1_bt_trials$solution == 1L,
  task1_bt_trials$correct_image,
  task1_bt_trials$wrong_image
)
task1_bt_expected_opt2 <- if_else(
  task1_bt_trials$solution == 2L,
  task1_bt_trials$correct_image,
  task1_bt_trials$wrong_image
)

  nrow(task1_bt_trials) == 2394,
  all(task1_bt_trials$stimulus == task1_bt_trials$correct_image),
  all(task1_bt_trials$recorded_correct ==

    paste0(task1_bt_expected_opt1, "_")

    paste0(task1_bt_expected_opt2, "_")

      as.integer(vistype == "bivariate_range"),
    match_triple_CI = matches_target * as.integer(vistype == "triple_CI"),
    match_uncert_markers = matches_target *
      as.integer(vistype == "uncert_markers"),
    match_N170 = matches_target * as.integer(pattern == "N170"),
    match_P3 = matches_target * as.integer(pattern == "P3"),
    match_position_c = matches_target * position_c

  group_by(choice_set) |>

    matching = sum(matches_target),
    .groups = "drop"

  all(task1_bt_choice_counts$alternatives == 2L),
  all(task1_bt_choice_counts$selected == 1L),
  all(task1_bt_choice_counts$matching == 1L),
  nlevels(task1_bt_choices$candidate_image) == 30L

    match_adjacent + match_animation +
    match_bivariate_corner + match_bivariate_range +
    match_triple_CI + match_uncert_markers +
    match_N170 + match_P3 + match_position_c +

Model: Conditional logistic paired-choice model with one stratum per participant–trial.


Image effects: One shared fixed attractiveness parameter was estimated for each candidate image across matching and nonmatching roles.


Adjustment: Matching-candidate effects were adjusted for ERP pattern, presentation position, and whether the candidate was shown second.

Multiplicity: Individual comparison p values and intervals are unadjusted; the joint robust Wald test is reported below.











NoteTerms explanation






Conditional: The model compares the two candidate images within the same participant’s trial. It uses the fact that exactly one candidate was selected and removes the separate baseline for each trial. The term does not refer to an experimental condition.
Stratum: A stratum is one participant–trial choice set. It contains two rows: one for the matching candidate and one for the nonmatching candidate. The model compares candidates within this set, not candidates from different trials.





Sensitivity-analysis conclusion
After accounting for candidate-image attractiveness, option position, ERP pattern, and presentation position, the joint participant-clustered Wald test indicated that visualization type changed preference for the matching candidate, \(\chi^2(6) =
12.81\), p = 0.0461. These individual intervals are unadjusted for the six comparisons. The sensitivity analysis therefore supports the primary model’s pattern while separating matching performance from images’ general tendency to be selected; it does not replace the primary mixed-effects accuracy analysis.
